notes: This retelling selects and orders events to emphasize remembered covenant and deliverance. Its sequence should be heard on its own terms alongside Exodus.

Verse 18 follows the read form, “foot”; the written form has “feet.” “His word” in verse 19 can refer to Joseph’s word or God’s promise. Verse 22 retains “bind”; Joseph’s authority over princes is not reduced to teaching them.

The poem explicitly says God turned the Egyptians’ hearts. Verse 28 says “they did not rebel,” but does not identify the plural subject; proposals include the divine messengers. The negative is retained.
vocabulary: Covenant
A binding relationship or commitment; here the ancestral promise God remembers.
Staff of bread
Bread pictured as a support on which life depends.
YAH
The short form of the divine name, retained in “Praise YAH.”

sections.1: We have sinned with our ancestors

notes: “Wasting” describes an affliction sent despite the granted request. The Hebrew does not require the later expression “leanness of soul” to mean spiritual emptiness.

“The dead” may refer to dead beings or lifeless deities. Phinehas’s intervention recalls the violent action in Numbers 25. “His spirit” in verse 33 can refer to God or Moses; the next clause concerns Moses’s rash speech.
The psalm recounts commands to destroy peoples and the sacrifice of sons and daughters. These actions remain explicit in the translation.
Verse 45 follows the read form’s plural expressions of faithful love, rendered collectively. Verse 48 closes Book Four of Psalms.
vocabulary: Sea of Reeds
The Hebrew name traditionally rendered “Red Sea”; the wording here preserves the source designation.
Breach
A gap in a defensive wall; Moses is pictured standing in it to avert destruction.
Righteousness
Right standing or conduct; here the assessment credited to Phinehas’s act.

notes: The Hebrew has “the sea,” where some translations give “south” to complete four compass points. “Sea” is retained.
The thanksgiving refrain repeats in verses 8, 15, 21, and 31. The rescue clauses vary: “rescued,” “saved,” and “brought them out.” These differences are retained.
The source includes inverted-nun scribal marks at these verses. They are preserved in the source records; their significance is uncertain, and they do not add spoken words.
vocabulary: Death’s shadow
An expression for profound darkness with deathly associations.
Harbor
The rare Hebrew destination term is understood here as a haven for the ships.

sections.1: Steadfast praise and a plea for victory

notes: This psalm reuses material also found in Psalms 57 and 60, with differences of wording. Its separate title is included in verse 1; Hebrew body labels are one higher.
“My glory” can refer to the speaker’s whole honorable self or poetic voice. “In his holiness” can also be understood as “in his sanctuary.” The territorial images proclaim rule and subjugation.
vocabulary: Ruler’s staff
A symbol of governing authority associated here with Judah.
Thrown sandal
An ancient gesture of possession or contempt; the exact force is debated.

notes: The switch from plural attackers to a singular target is abrupt. Some read these curses as the speaker’s petition; others as hostile words being quoted. The Hebrew supplies no explicit quotation introduction. The translation leaves the transition visible without adding “they say.”
The curses extend to wife, children, and ancestors. Their severity is preserved as the poem’s speech, not converted into a general instruction to readers.
The LORD’s place at the needy person’s right hand reverses the accuser’s position in verse 6.
vocabulary: Accuser
A legal or personal adversary. The Hebrew word here does not require the proper name Satan.
Office
A position of responsibility or oversight.

sections.1: A royal declaration and a priestly oath

notes: “The LORD” represents the divine name; “my lord” is the speaker’s address to a superior. The psalm does not name that addressee here.

Verse 3 has compressed, difficult syntax: voluntary people, holy splendor, dawn’s womb, and the dew of youth. Verse 4’s formula is rendered “in the manner of Melchizedek”; its precise relation to that priest-king is debated. These lines require further editorial review.
“The Lord” in verse 5 renders Adonai. The final drinking scene does not explicitly identify its subject or explain how it connects to the preceding battle.
vocabulary: Footstool
Here a royal image of defeated enemies placed beneath a ruler’s feet.
Melchizedek
The priest-king named in Genesis 14; his name remains untranslated here.

notes: After “Praise YAH,” the Hebrew poetic units follow the twenty-two letters of the alphabet. Verses 9 and 10 each contain three units. The English preserves the units without pretending to reproduce the alphabetic pattern.
vocabulary: Covenant
God’s binding commitment to his people, remembered and established forever in this poem.
Fear of the LORD
Reverent fear expressed in practiced obedience; the poem connects understanding with doing.

notes: Like Psalm 111, this is an alphabetic poem with twenty-two poetic units. It portrays the flourishing of a righteous person in wisdom poetry; the statements remain in their poetic form.
“Gracious, compassionate, and righteous” may describe the upright person or God as the source of light. The translation takes the former connection while preserving the echo of Psalm 111.
vocabulary: Horn
An animal’s horn used as an image of strength and honor.

sections.1: From the heights to the refuse heap

notes: The repeated downward and upward movements connect divine height with care for people in low places. Verse 9 portrays a particular reversal of childlessness, not a timetable attached to every reader’s life.
vocabulary: Refuse heap
A place of discarded waste, marking extreme poverty in the image.

notes: The poem addresses sea, river, mountains, and earth as responsive participants in Israel’s deliverance. Its animal comparisons and changing addresses remain intact.
vocabulary: Sanctuary
A holy place belonging to God; here Judah itself is described this way.
Flint
A very hard stone, making its transformation into flowing water striking.

notes: Each call to trust is followed by “their help and their shield.” This shift can be heard as a communal response; it has not been changed to “your.”
The contrast between the dead in silence and the living who bless YAH is preserved without adding an explanation from later passages.
vocabulary: Idols
Manufactured objects of worship, described here by their materials and powerless body parts.

notes: The relation of believing and speaking can be read in several ways. This draft takes it as trust continuing even during the speaker’s alarmed cries.
The word rendered “costly” can mean precious or highly valued. In this prayer of rescue it conveys that the death of God’s faithful ones is no light matter.
vocabulary: Sheol
The realm of the dead in Hebrew poetic language.
Cup and vows
The singer describes public thanksgiving through a raised cup and fulfilled promises; the precise cup ritual is not specified.

notes: The nations are invited to praise because of God’s mighty faithful love “toward us.” The movement from the particular community to all peoples is retained.
vocabulary: Faithfulness
Reliability and truth; paired here with faithful love.

sections.1: The rejected stone and the open gate

notes: The repeated verb in verses 10–12 is rendered “cut them off.” Verse 13 abruptly addresses a singular opponent. “My song” in verse 14 represents a traditional reading; the Hebrew expression can also be understood in terms of might or defense.

“Cornerstone” renders the stone’s new chief position. Verse 27 is difficult: it may describe binding a festival offering with cords or a festival procession with branches reaching the altar. The draft retains binding, cords, and altar horns and records the alternative.
vocabulary: YAH
The short form of the divine name, used repeatedly in this psalm alongside the full name rendered LORD.
Altar horns
Projections at the corners of an altar.

notes: The poem has twenty-two stanzas of eight verses. In Hebrew every verse of a stanza starts with that stanza’s letter. The letter headings mark this structure; the English does not reproduce the acrostic. Repeated terms and pleas have not been compressed.

“To the end” in verse 33 can also be understood as fully or as reward. Verse 38’s relative clause may qualify the promise or the servant who fears God. Verse 56’s “this” has no explicit noun; the draft avoids naming an unstated reward.
A heart thick as fat suggests insensitivity. Verse 79 follows the read form “those who know”; the written form can be read “and they will know.”

Verse 96’s “perfection” is a difficult term for completeness or an end. Verse 126 can mean it is time for the LORD to act or time to act for the LORD. Verse 128 retains the Hebrew’s sweeping, somewhat awkward claim about all precepts in every matter.
Verses 147 and 161 follow the read form “word,” rather than written “words.” “The sum” in verse 160 can also be read “the beginning.”
The final lost-sheep plea stands beside the claim not to have forgotten the commands. The poem does not resolve that tension with an added conclusion.
vocabulary: Instruction terms

“Instruction” renders torah; “testimonies,” edot; “precepts,” piqqudim; “decrees,” huqqim; “commands,” mitswot; “judgments,” mishpatim; “word,” davar; and “utterance” or, where promised fulfillment is in view, “promise,” imrah. These overlapping terms present several aspects of God’s direction.
Wineskin in smoke
A leather container exposed to smoke, an image of shriveling or distress.
Life in my hand; guarantor
The first is an image of constant danger. A guarantor takes responsibility for another’s security or obligation.

sections.1: Peace among those who want war

notes: This begins the collection of fifteen Songs of Ascents, Psalms 120–134. Their exact original setting is not specified by the title. Meshech and Kedar represent widely separated places; the lament need not describe one literal address.
vocabulary: Broom wood
Wood from a desert shrub used for hot-burning coals.

sections.1: The guardian who does not sleep

notes: The title says “for ascents,” a slight variation on the collection’s usual title. The mountain question is answered by naming the maker of heaven and earth. Verse 3 is phrased as a wish; verse 4 gives an assurance.
vocabulary: Guardian
The repeated Hebrew root means keep, watch, or guard. Its recurrence holds the psalm together.

notes: The poem links Jerusalem’s joined construction, gathered tribes, royal judgment, and peace. Its Hebrew plays on the sounds of Jerusalem, peace, and security.
vocabulary: Testimony
An established obligation or attestation; here connected with Israel’s going up to give thanks.

notes: The comparison uses male and female slaves and their masters’ hands. It depicts dependence while retaining the unequal social relationships in the source.
vocabulary: Favor
Gracious attention or mercy, sought repeatedly by a community worn down by contempt.

sections.1: The trap broke and we escaped

notes: The repeated “if” clauses describe what would have happened without help. The flood and swallowing images are not turned into a literal event report.
vocabulary: Hunters’ trap
A snare for birds; its breaking pictures the community’s escape.

notes: The reason given for ending wicked rule is that the righteous might otherwise reach out to wrongdoing. The political and moral pressure remain connected.
vocabulary: Scepter
A ruler’s staff, here representing wicked power over an allotted land.

notes: The poem remembers restoration and then asks for restoration again. “Fortunes” can also evoke the return of captives; the draft does not restrict the expression to one aspect of recovery.
vocabulary: Negev
The dry southern region, where normally dry channels can suddenly fill with water.

notes: The last clause may mean God gives his beloved sleep, or gives to his beloved while they sleep. The draft takes sleep as the gift and retains the alternative here.
The household is portrayed through sons, arrows, a quiver, and speaking with enemies at the city gate. The masculine family and public setting remain visible.
vocabulary: Gate
The city’s public place for legal and civic dealings as well as entry and defense.

sections.1: Blessing at the table and in Zion

notes: The blessing moves from enjoyed labor and household fruitfulness to Jerusalem and all Israel. The wife, children, and generations remain concrete parts of the poem.
vocabulary: Olive shoots
Young growth around an olive tree, an image of children gathered around a table.

notes: Verse 3 follows the read form’s singular “furrow.” In verse 6 the verb may refer to pulling grass or its shooting up; both readings emphasize growth that withers before a useful harvest.
vocabulary: Plowers on my back
An image of severe bodily oppression, not merely an inconvenience.

notes: The poem moves from individual guilt and waiting to Israel’s hope for redemption. Forgiveness leads to fear of God in verse 4; the connection is retained.
vocabulary: Redemption
Release or rescue; here explicitly from Israel’s wrongs.

notes: The child is weaned, not nursing. The repeated comparison portrays a quieted self resting with its mother, while the final line turns the image inward.
vocabulary: Haughty eyes
An image of pride or looking down on others.

sections.1: A dwelling, a covenant, and a lamp

notes: “It” is not explicitly named in this verse; the ark in verse 8 supplies the likely context. Ephrathah and the fields of Jaar remain named without expanding an uncertain itinerary.
The promise about descendants includes an explicit covenant condition in verse 12. Horn, lamp, clothing, and blossoming crown carry the royal imagery.
vocabulary: Ark
The sacred chest associated with God’s presence and strength; not a boat in this context.
Horn and lamp
Images of royal strength and continuing dynasty.

notes: The repeated downward flow connects oil and dew. Hermon’s dew on Zion is poetic imagery; the translation does not replace it with a geographical explanation.
vocabulary: Aaron
Israel’s priestly ancestor, named in the image of oil flowing over head, beard, and robes.

notes: The call addresses temple servants at night; the final blessing addresses a singular “you.” “Toward the sanctuary” in verse 2 can also be understood as “in holiness.”
vocabulary: Sanctuary
The holy place toward which worshipers lift their hands in this reading.

sections.1: The living God and powerless idols

notes: The idol description resembles Psalm 115 but has its own wording, especially the absence of breath in verse 17. Those differences remain.
vocabulary: Treasured possession
Something specially chosen and valued; here Israel in relation to God.

notes: Every verse retains the full refrain. The repeated faithful-love claim accompanies creation, food, rescue, and the violent overthrow of enemies; the translation does not omit the difficult pairings.
vocabulary: All flesh
Living creatures broadly, not only human beings.

notes: The speaker invokes loss of skill and speech on himself if he forgets Jerusalem. “Its skill” supplies the implied object of the right hand’s forgetting.

The Hebrew describes Babylon as devastated or destined for devastation. The final blessing voices the exiles’ retaliatory desire against Babylon’s little children. Its violence is preserved as the speaker’s speech; no command to the reader is added.
vocabulary: Poplars
A riverside tree identification; “willows” is another traditional rendering.

notes: “Gods” can also be understood as heavenly beings or rulers. Verse 2 literally says “you have magnified your utterance above all your name.” The draft unpacks “name” as what it proclaims. This clause is unusually compressed; some translations rearrange it to exalt both name and word above everything. This draft preserves the more difficult relation in the pinned Hebrew.
vocabulary: Work of your hands
A creation image applied to the speaker’s life and circumstances.

notes: The bodily and textile images include kidneys, womb, frame, embroidery, and an unformed body. Verse 14’s verb conveys being wondrously distinguished or set apart. These lines are not expanded into a scientific description.

The draft follows the written negative, “not one,” in a difficult clause about days formed and written. The read form has “for him/it,” allowing a different construction such as one among them being assigned to him. The relation of the clauses remains debated; both forms are retained in the source ledger.

“Thoughts” in verse 17 can also mean friends. Verse 20 is textually difficult; “your name” makes explicit the likely object of taking in vain. The hatred and death wish in verses 19–22 remain beside the final request for self-examination. “Hurtful way” can also suggest a way of pain or idolatry.
vocabulary: Sheol
The realm of the dead, paired here with heaven as the opposite vertical extreme.
Kidneys
An ancient bodily image of the inner person, retained alongside the womb image.

notes: The separate Hebrew title is included in verse 1; subsequent Hebrew body labels are one higher. Selah is retained at verses 3, 5, and 8.

Verse 8’s “rise high” clause is compressed; it may be a consequence or another wish. Verses 9, 10, and 12 follow the read forms for “cover,” “fall,” and “I know.” The coals and pits remain actual images of destructive judgment.
vocabulary: Selah
A traditional poetic or musical marker whose precise function is uncertain.

sections.1: Guard my mouth and my heart

notes: These are difficult Hebrew lines. The draft takes the righteous person’s correction as welcome oil, but the last clause of verse 5 and the judges/cliff scene in verse 6 remain uncertain. Verse 7 says “our bones.” Verse 10’s net pronoun is singular in Hebrew; English “their” connects the trap with the wicked without claiming a certain original referent.
vocabulary: Evening offering
A regular act of worship used here as a comparison for raised hands in prayer.
Sheol
The realm of the dead, pictured as having a mouth receiving scattered bones.

notes: The separate title names a cave but does not identify which episode of David’s life. It is included in verse 1; later Hebrew labels are one higher. “Confinement” in verse 7 need not mean a literal jail.
vocabulary: Maskil
A traditional psalm designation, possibly connected with skill or instruction; its precise musical or literary force is uncertain.

sections.1: Teach me the way to walk

notes: Verse 9’s final expression is unusual, literally involving covering “to you”; the draft understands seeking shelter. The good spirit leading on level ground retains a concrete path image.
vocabulary: Pit
A poetic name or image for the realm of death.

notes: Verse 2 follows “my people,” not the variant-like rendering “peoples.” Verses 12–14 are taken as wishes for the community. Their connection to verse 11 is compressed, and other constructions are possible. The cattle may be laden, pregnant, or strong for carrying; “no breach” and “no going out” can describe civic security or livestock loss. The draft keeps the difficult images and records these alternatives.
vocabulary: Right hand of lies
The right hand evokes pledged trust or an oath, here marked as false.
